description: Kivu releaf Restoration uses NASA satellite data and GIS technologies to identify land degradation and recommend sustainable restoration strategies through agroforestry, reforestation and natural regeneration, helping mountain communities adapt to climate change and protect their soils and water resources.
summary: Kivu smart is a geospatial decision-support tool designed to help smallholder farmers in Kalehe, South Kivu, adapt their agricultural practices to changing environmental conditions. By combining NASA Earth observation data with local soil and crop information, the platform aims to assess soil conditions, rainfall patterns, vegetation changes, and erosion risks. It will help farmers explore suitable crop rotation strategies and soil conservation practices based on the characteristics of their land and their priorities. The goal is to support more informed agricultural decisions, improve soil health, conserve water, and strengthen the long-term resilience of farming systems.
details:
What exactly does it do?

Kivu smart is a dynamic decision-support system for large-scale forest landscape restoration. More specifically:

  • Digitizes and analyzes mountain and forest ecosystems in the Kalehe Territory and the periphery of Kahuzi-Biega National Park (KBNP) by leveraging multi-sensor satellite data from NASA and Copernicus (100% drone-free).
  • Identifies optimal areas for restoration (protective reforestation, agroforestry, assisted natural regeneration) based on slope, vegetation health, soil moisture, and climate stress indicators.
  • Prescribes tailored interventions according to soil conditions and local tree species (such as Podocarpus, Maesopsis eminii, Calliandra, and Grevillea) to maximize tree survival and growth.
  • Monitors phenology and degradation of forests and agricultural lands over time (2015–2026) to ensure sustainability and alignment with REDD+ requirements.
  • Centralizes information on an interactive web platform (Streamlit Cloud) so conservation agencies (ICCN), local authorities (Kalehe ETDs), NGOs, and farmer groups can plan and execute targeted restoration campaigns.

How does it work?

The process follows a structured and reproducible workflow:

  • Geospatial and topographic digitization: Utilization of NASA SRTM / NASADEM elevation models (30 m) and geographic boundaries to map steep slopes (> 30–35%) and hydrographic networks of the Kalehe Territory.
  • Satellite and climate data analysis: Continuous ingestion via Google Earth Engine of optical series from NASA HLS and Sentinel-2 (NDVI, bare soil indices), Sentinel-1 SAR radar (cloud-penetrating), SMAP L4 soil moisture data, GPM IMERG extreme rainfall, and NASA POWER climatology.
  • GIS-AHP multi-criteria modeling: An Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) algorithm, validated by local experts with a strict consistency ratio (CR < 0.10), intersects all variables to generate suitability scores (0–100) for each restoration scenario.
  • Agronomic and forestry prescription: The application generates tailored recommendations for each plot (species selection, planting densities, cost estimates, and REDD+ carbon gain estimates).
  • Participatory execution and monitoring: Maps and technical datasheets (GeoJSON/CSV) are used on the ground, coupled with participatory validation alongside local agronomists and committees in Kalehe, while the platform continues to monitor vegetation cover evolution.

AHP Weight Matrices & Criteria Integration

The Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) model relies on pairwise comparison evaluations (Saaty scale 1 to 9) conducted by 30 local experts from South Kivu, ensuring strict mathematical consistency (Consistency Ratio CR < 0.10).

Cette pondération accorde une importance prépondérante aux facteurs topographiques et d'accessibilité locaux, en particulier la pente (représentant jusqu'à 63,33 % du poids pour la RNA et 37,44 % pour le reboisement pur) ainsi que la proximité des rivières, des villages et des zones agricoles.

Les données satellitaires de la NASA (comme SMAP pour l'humidité du sol, GPM IMERG pour les précipitations et FIRMS pour les feux) possèdent des résolutions spatiales plus larges, s'étendant de 9 km à 50 km. Afin de préserver la précision spatiale fine du découpage à 30 mètres géré par l'AHP, ces indicateurs régionaux n'altèrent pas directement la somme pondérée des critères. Ils interviennent sous forme de masques booléens de contrainte (pour exclure les zones sujettes aux brûlis) ou d'ajustements dynamiques de risque (pour intégrer l'érosion et le stress hydrique en temps réel), articulant ainsi la précision du terrain avec les flux satellitaires récurrents.

What are the benefits?

  • Environmental: Restores a highly vulnerable mountain ecosystem, combats soil desertification, reduces water erosion (currently at 44.35 t/ha/year), and improves water retention and recharge of aquifers tributary to Lake Kivu.
  • Social: Secures water supply and land fertility for Kalehe communities, reduces the risk of deadly landslides, and mitigates conflicts related to pressure on land and resources in KBNP.
  • Economic: Optimizes efficiency and success rates of reforestation projects and REDD+ initiatives, protecting subsistence agriculture and local economic activities. The model relies on a free, open-source decision-support tool ensuring the long-term sustainability of environmental investments.

What do you hope to accomplish?

In the short term, our goal is to validate the decision-support model on pilot plots in Kalehe Territory and along the border of KBNP, providing local stakeholders with an immediate operational tool. In the long term, we seek to reverse forest degradation across the entire region, secure water resources and habitats for endangered species, and establish a reproducible open-source geospatial model for the entire Albertine Rift.

Integrates Future Climate Change Projections:

Incorporates NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 climate projections to assess future environmental vulnerability under three climate scenarios (SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, and SSP5-8.5) for 2030, 2050, and 2080. The system evaluates projected changes in temperature, precipitation, and water stress to anticipate shifts in restoration suitability, identify climate-resilient tree species, and recommend adaptive restoration strategies. This enables stakeholders to prioritize interventions not only according to current environmental conditions but also their long-term resilience to climate change.

Technical Stack & Data Sources

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

  • Gemini AI: Generation and development of geospatial processing scripts (Google Earth Engine, Python), GIS-AHP multi-criteria modeling for Kalehe Territory, and structuring of technical and scientific deliverables.
  • Claude AI: Cleaning, optimization, debugging, and review of programming algorithms to ensure code stability and reproducibility.
  • ChatGPT: Initial analysis of the environmental framework, structuring of the platform's technical architecture, and generation of visual illustrations.
  • Perplexity AI: In-depth literature review, verification of scientific sources, and bibliographic referencing on forest landscape restoration in South Kivu.
  • GitHub Copilot: Code drafting assistance in the editor (VS Code), error detection, and inspection of code block structure and size.
